The exact location of the crash has not been determined, because ocean currents probably caused the bodies and debris to drift in the days since the crash. Two key pieces of evidence -- the flight data and cockpit voice recorders -- remain missing and could lie on the ocean floor.  Map of Flight 447's flight path » . Brazilian officials emphasized Monday that finding bodies was their priority. The French are in charge of finding the black boxes, and a submarine was en route as part of that mission. Fourteen aircraft -- 12 Brazilian and two French -- were participating, along with five Brazilian ships and one French frigate. In Washington, a U.S. defense official said the U.S. Navy will contribute two high-tech acoustic devices to listen for emergency beacons still operating in deep water. The "towed pinger locators," which help search for emergency beacons on downed aircraft to a maximum depth of 20,000 feet, will be placed aboard two French tugs that are part of the search efforts, the official said. Recovery of bodies and debris is significant not only for families but also for crash investigators, said Mary Schiavo, a former inspector general for the U.S. Department of Transportation. "Even if they don't find anything else, they can get some very important clues from the pieces that they do find and from the human remains," she said Saturday.  Watch an explanation of what could have caused the crash » . She said investigators would be able to tell whether there was an explosion from possible residue on the bodies or other items. Or, if water is found in the lungs of victims, investigators would know that the plane went down intact, she said. Investigators in Paris said Saturday that the Air France flight sent 24 automated error messages about four minutes before it crashed. The messages suggest the plane may have been flying too fast or too slow through severe thunderstorms it encountered before the crash, officials said. Schiavo said four minutes "was a very long time" for automated signals to be sent from the plane. Investigators also reported that the airline had failed to replace a part as recommended by the manufacturer, Airbus. Airbus had advised airlines to update part of the equipment that monitors speed, known as pitot tubes. The recommendation was a result of technological developments and improvements, an Airbus spokesman said. The change was not mandatory, and the spokesman would not comment on Air France's failure to follow the advice. CNN's Karl Penhaul, Richard Quest, Helena DeMoura and Barbara Starr contributed to this report.

Recovery teams have also found several items confirmed to have come from Air France Flight 447. Military officials said Monday evening that the bodies were found floating about 440 kilometers (273 miles) northeast of the Fernando de Noronha archipelago, off Brazil’s northeastern coast.

Air France Flight 447 disappeared over the Atlantic early on June 1. The aircraft was traveling from Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, to Paris, France, with 228 passengers and crew members aboard.

Earlier Monday, the military had said that 16 bodies had been recovered. Items found in the same area Saturday were confirmed to have come from the jet, including pieces of the aircraft’s wing section, luggage, and a leather briefcase containing an airplane ticket with a reservation code for the doomed flight, Brazilian air force spokesman Jorge Amaral said.

The exact location of the crash has not been determined, as ocean currents likely caused the bodies and debris to drift in the days following the crash.

Two key pieces of evidence — the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder — remain missing and could be lying on the ocean floor.

The section of the ocean where the debris and bodies have been found ranges from 6,000 to 8,000 meters deep, or about 19,700 to 26,250 feet. The search area spans 200,000 square kilometers (77,220 square miles), nearly the size of Romania.

Brazilian officials emphasized Monday that recovering bodies remained their priority. French authorities are leading the search for the black boxes, and a submarine was en route as part of that effort.

In Washington, a U.S. defense official said the U.S. Navy would provide two high-tech acoustic devices to listen for emergency beacons that may still be operating in deep water. The “towed pinger locators,” which are used to search for emergency beacons on downed aircraft at depths of up to 20,000 feet, will be placed aboard two French tugs involved in the search, the official said.

The recovery of bodies and debris is significant not only for the victims’ families but also for crash investigators, said Mary Schiavo, a former inspector general for the U.S. Department of Transportation.

“Even if they don’t find anything else, they can get some very important clues from the pieces that they do find and from the human remains,” she said Saturday.

Schiavo said investigators would be able to determine whether there had been an explosion by examining possible residue on the bodies or other recovered items. Alternatively, if water is found in the victims’ lungs, investigators would know that the plane went down intact, she said.

Schiavo said four minutes was “a very long time” for automated signals to be sent from the plane.

Investigators also reported that the airline had not replaced a part as recommended by the manufacturer, Airbus. Airbus had advised airlines to update part of the equipment that monitors speed, known as pitot tubes.

An Airbus spokesman said the recommendation resulted from technological developments and improvements. The change was not mandatory, and the spokesman would not comment on Air France’s failure to follow the advice.

CNN’s Karl Penhaul, Richard Quest, Helena DeMoura, and Barbara Starr contributed to this report.

**Recovered Wreckage and Bodies Offer First Clues in Air France Flight 447 Disaster**

*By [News Desk]*

In the days after Air France Flight 447 vanished over the Atlantic Ocean, search crews from Brazil and France began recovering pieces of wreckage and victims’ remains from a vast stretch of open sea, offering the first physical evidence in one of modern aviation’s most confounding disasters.

The Airbus A330, carrying 228 people from Rio de Janeiro to Paris, disappeared early on June 1, 2009, after flying into a zone of powerful storms over the equatorial Atlantic. The aircraft had sent a series of automated maintenance messages indicating system failures before contact was lost, but no distress call was received from the crew.

Brazilian military teams, operating from aircraft and ships, located debris roughly hundreds of miles off Brazil’s northeast coast. Among the items recovered were aircraft seats, luggage, oxygen masks, sections of the aircraft’s interior, and structural components believed to be from the Air France jet. Searchers also recovered bodies from the sea, which were transported to shore for identification and examination.

French authorities confirmed that the recovered material was consistent with Flight 447, while cautioning that the debris alone would not explain why the aircraft went down.

## Brazil Leads Search in Remote Atlantic Waters

Brazil’s air force and navy took the lead in the initial search and recovery effort because the crash occurred closer to Brazil than to Africa or Europe. Patrol aircraft swept enormous areas of ocean, directing navy ships toward floating debris fields scattered by currents and weather.

The search zone presented major challenges. Flight 447 disappeared in a remote portion of the Atlantic known for deep water, rough seas, and rapidly changing weather. Debris was spread over a wide area, complicating recovery and making it difficult to determine exactly where the aircraft entered the water.

Brazilian officials said the recovery effort focused both on locating victims and preserving evidence for investigators. Ships collected wreckage carefully, while aircraft continued searching for additional debris fields. The Brazilian military also coordinated with French investigators and Air France representatives as recovered items were catalogued.

## France Sends Ships, Aircraft and Investigators

France, as the country where Air France is based and where the aircraft was registered, launched its own investigation through the Bureau d’Enquêtes et d’Analyses, or BEA, the French air accident investigation agency.

French ships and aircraft joined the search, and technical teams began analyzing the automated messages transmitted by the aircraft shortly before it vanished. Those messages indicated multiple system faults, including issues related to flight controls and airspeed data, but investigators repeatedly warned that such messages were not enough to determine the cause of the crash.

French officials also focused on locating the aircraft’s flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder — the “black boxes” — which were believed to be resting on the ocean floor. The recorders were considered essential to understanding what happened in the cockpit during the flight’s final minutes.

## U.S. Navy Provides Undersea Search Assistance

The United States Navy assisted the recovery effort by providing specialized equipment to help detect signals from the aircraft’s underwater locator beacons. These beacons, attached to the flight recorders, were designed to emit acoustic “pings” for a limited period after contact with water.

U.S. Navy towed pinger locator equipment was deployed to aid the French-led underwater search. The task was extremely difficult because the suspected crash zone sat above rugged undersea terrain, with depths reaching several thousand meters. Search crews faced a race against time, as the beacon batteries were expected to last only about 30 days.

The Navy’s assistance underscored the international scope of the operation. With debris found on the surface and the main wreckage believed to be far below, investigators needed both surface recovery teams and advanced sonar and acoustic equipment to continue the search beneath the Atlantic.

## Investigators Urge Caution

French investigators stressed that it was too soon to identify a single cause. BEA officials said the aircraft’s automated messages showed a sequence of failures, but they did not amount to a full account of the accident.

Paul-Louis Arslanian, then head of the BEA, told reporters that investigators had only “partial” information and warned against speculation. He said the inquiry would examine all possibilities, including weather, aircraft systems, crew actions, and the sequence of technical faults reported before the plane disappeared.

A particular area of interest quickly became the aircraft’s airspeed sensors, known as pitot tubes. In the aftermath of the crash, Air France and Airbus faced questions about whether icing or malfunctioning airspeed sensors could have contributed to the loss of reliable speed readings. Investigators, however, emphasized that even if airspeed data problems occurred, that would not by itself explain the loss of the aircraft.

Airbus issued safety reminders to operators about procedures for handling unreliable airspeed indications, while Air France accelerated replacement of certain pitot probes on its A330 and A340 fleets. Officials said those actions were precautionary and should not be interpreted as proof of causation.

## A Difficult Identification Process

As bodies were recovered, Brazilian authorities began the process of identification, working with dental records, fingerprints, and DNA samples provided by families. Victims came from more than 30 countries, making coordination between governments and consulates a major part of the aftermath.

Families of passengers gathered in Brazil and France, awaiting confirmation and demanding answers. Air France offered support to relatives, while French and Brazilian authorities provided updates on the search. Memorial services were held in both countries as the scale of the tragedy became clear.

## The Central Mystery Remains

Despite the recovery of floating wreckage and some victims, the central mystery remained unresolved in the immediate aftermath: why did a modern long-haul aircraft, flown by an experienced crew, vanish without a distress call?

Investigators said the final answer would depend heavily on locating and analyzing the flight recorders and reconstructing the aircraft’s final moments. Until then, officials warned, every theory remained incomplete.

The disaster became one of the most complex aviation investigations of its time, involving deep-ocean search technology, international cooperation, and intense scrutiny of aircraft systems and pilot response under extreme conditions. For the families of the 228 people aboard, the recovery of wreckage marked only the beginning of a long search for answers.

**Search Crews Recover Debris, Bodies From Air France Flight 447 in Atlantic**

*RIO DE JANEIRO/PARIS —* Recovery teams searching the Atlantic Ocean have found wreckage and bodies from Air France Flight 447, the Airbus A330 that disappeared June 1 while flying from Rio de Janeiro to Paris with 228 people aboard, officials said.

Brazilian military aircraft and naval vessels, joined by French ships and aircraft, have been sweeping a remote area of the Atlantic several hundred miles off Brazil’s northeastern coast. The operation has focused on locating floating debris and recovering evidence that could help investigators determine why the aircraft went down.

Authorities said search teams have recovered aircraft parts, personal belongings and other debris consistent with the missing jet. Among the items reported found were sections of the aircraft’s structure, seats, luggage, a life vest and other floating material. Crews also spotted fuel slicks in the area. Brazilian officials later confirmed the recovery of bodies from the ocean.

The most significant pieces of wreckage were being documented, photographed and transported for examination by investigators. French aviation accident investigators are leading the inquiry, with assistance from Brazilian authorities and Airbus specialists.

Flight 447 left Rio de Janeiro’s Galeão International Airport on the evening of May 31 and was scheduled to arrive at Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport the next morning. The aircraft disappeared from radar and failed to make scheduled contact after entering an area of strong equatorial thunderstorms over the Atlantic.

Investigators have said the aircraft sent automated maintenance messages before contact was lost, indicating multiple system faults, including possible problems with airspeed readings and electrical systems. Officials cautioned that the messages alone do not establish the cause of the crash.

A major priority remains locating the aircraft’s flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder, commonly known as black boxes. The devices are believed to be on the ocean floor in very deep water, making the search difficult. French authorities have deployed specialized equipment to listen for acoustic signals from the recorders’ underwater locator beacons, which typically transmit for about 30 days.

The search area lies in a vast and challenging stretch of ocean, with deep seabed terrain and shifting currents that can scatter debris over long distances. Officials said the recovery effort could take weeks or longer.

All 228 people aboard Flight 447 — 216 passengers and 12 crew members — are presumed dead. The passengers included citizens from several countries, with large numbers from Brazil, France and Germany.

Air France has said it is cooperating fully with investigators and assisting families of the victims. French and Brazilian officials said the recovery of debris and bodies marks an important step, but determining the cause of the disaster will depend on further evidence, especially the flight recorders.
